We reduce \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) to \(I_3\) using column transformations.

Apply \(C_1 \to C_1 - 2C_2\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

Apply \(C_1 \to C_1 + 3C_3\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

Apply \(C_2 \to C_2 - 3C_3\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I_3\).

Hence \(A\) is reduced to \(I_3\) by column transformations.

We reduce \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) to \(I_3\) using row transformations.

\(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1,\ R_3 \to R_3 - R_1\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(R_3 \to R_3 - R_2\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(R_3 \to -R_3\), then \(R_1 \to R_1 - R_3,\ R_2 \to R_2 - R_3\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I_3\).

Hence \(A\) is reduced to \(I_3\) by row transformations.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (1)(1) - (0)(0) = 1 \neq 0\).

Since \(|A| \neq 0\), the matrix is nonsingular, hence invertible.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (1)(1) - (1)(1) = 0\).

Since \(|A| = 0\), the matrix is singular, hence NOT invertible.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (1)(3) - (2)(3) = 3 - 6 = -3 \neq 0\).

Since \(|A| \neq 0\), the matrix is nonsingular, hence invertible.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 10 & 15 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (2)(15) - (3)(10) = 30 - 30 = 0\).

Since \(|A| = 0\), the matrix is singular, hence NOT invertible.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\),
\(|A| = \cos\theta\cdot\cos\theta - \sin\theta\cdot(-\sin\theta) = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1 \neq 0\).

Since \(|A| = 1 \neq 0\), the matrix is nonsingular, hence invertible.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \sec\theta & \tan\theta \\ \tan\theta & \sec\theta \end{bmatrix}\),
\(|A| = \sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1 \neq 0\).

Since \(|A| = 1 \neq 0\), the matrix is nonsingular, hence invertible.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), expand along \(R_1\):
\(|A| = 3(1\cdot5 - 0\cdot4) - 4(1\cdot5 - 0\cdot1) + 3(1\cdot4 - 1\cdot1)\)
\(= 3(5) - 4(5) + 3(3) = 15 - 20 + 9 = 4 \neq 0\).

Since \(|A| \neq 0\), the matrix is nonsingular, hence invertible.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), rows \(R_1\) and \(R_3\) are identical.

A determinant with two identical rows equals \(0\), so \(|A| = 0\).

Since \(|A| = 0\), the matrix is singular, hence NOT invertible.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 4 & 6 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\), note \(R_3 = R_1 + R_2\), so the rows are dependent.

Expanding: \(|A| = 1(32-30) - 2(24-20) + 3(18-16) = 2 - 8 + 6 = 0\).

Since \(|A| = 0\), the matrix is singular, hence NOT invertible.

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\ (2\times3)\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\ (3\times2)\).

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1+2+3 & -1+4-6 \\ 1-2-3 & -1-4+6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ -4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(|AB| = (6)(1) - (-3)(-4) = 6 - 12 = -6 \neq 0\).

Since \(|AB| \neq 0\), \(AB\) is nonsingular, hence \(AB\) has an inverse.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & z \end{bmatrix}\) with \(x,y,z \neq 0\) (nonsingular).

Write \(A = IA\) and apply \(R_1 \to \tfrac{1}{x}R_1,\ R_2 \to \tfrac{1}{y}R_2,\ R_3 \to \tfrac{1}{z}R_3\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{x} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{y} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{1}{z} \end{bmatrix} A\).

Hence \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{x} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{y} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{1}{z} \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) take \(x=2,\ y=1,\ z=-1\):
\(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer has the \((2,2)\) entry as \(+\tfrac{1}{2}\); it should be \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) (our answer).]

\(AX = I\) means \(X = A^{-1}\) for \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(|A| = (1)(4) - (2)(3) = 4 - 6 = -2 \neq 0\).

\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(X = A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\,\text{adj}(A) = -\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ \tfrac{3}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (1)(3) - (-1)(2) = 3 + 2 = 5 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (2)(-1) - (1)(1) = -2 - 1 = -3 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1} = -\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (1)(7) - (3)(2) = 7 - 6 = 1 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -3 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -3 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 5 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (2)(7) - (-3)(5) = 14 + 15 = 29 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{29}\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (2)(4) - (1)(7) = 8 - 7 = 1 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ -7 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ -7 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -10 \\ 2 & -7 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (3)(-7) - (-10)(2) = -21 + 20 = -1 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 10 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1} = -\begin{bmatrix} -7 & 10 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -10 \\ 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed inverse has wrong signs on two adjoint entries; the correct inverse is below.]

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), expand along \(R_1\):
\(|A| = 2(4+6) + 3(4-9) + 3(-4-6) = 20 - 15 - 30 = -25 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

Cofactors: \(A_{11}=10,\ A_{12}=5,\ A_{13}=-10\); \(A_{21}=0,\ A_{22}=-5,\ A_{23}=-5\); \(A_{31}=-15,\ A_{32}=0,\ A_{33}=10\).

\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 & -15 \\ 5 & -5 & 0 \\ -10 & -5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1} = -\frac{1}{25}\begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 & -15 \\ 5 & -5 & 0 \\ -10 & -5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Here \(|A| = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

(i) Row transformations: write \(A = IA\). Apply \(R_1 \to \cos\theta\,R_1 + \sin\theta\,R_2\) and \(R_2 \to -\sin\theta\,R_1 + \cos\theta\,R_2\) (using \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\)); the left side becomes \(I\) and the right side becomes \(A^{-1}\).

(ii) Column transformations: write \(A = AI\) and apply the corresponding column operations \(C_1 \to \cos\theta\,C_1 + \sin\theta\,C_2\), \(C_2 \to -\sin\theta\,C_1 + \cos\theta\,C_2\).

Both methods give
\(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
(This is just \(A^{T}\), as expected since \(A\) is orthogonal.)

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2+9 & 0+3 \\ 1+6 & 0+2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 3 \\ 7 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), with \(|AB| = 22 - 21 = 1\).

\((AB)^{-1} = \frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -7 & 11 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -7 & 11 \end{bmatrix}\).

Verification: \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) (since \(|A|=1\)), \(B^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) (since \(|B|=1\)).

\(B^{-1}A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -7 & 11 \end{bmatrix} = (AB)^{-1}\).

Hence \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}\) is verified.

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = (4)(1) - (5)(2) = 4 - 10 = -6 \neq 0\).

\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{-6}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -5 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\).

Now \(A - 5I = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\).

So \(\frac{1}{6}(A - 5I) = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix} = A^{-1}\).

Hence \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}(A - 5I)\) is shown.

\(AX = B \Rightarrow X = A^{-1}B\), where \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(|A| = (1)(3) - (2)(-1) = 3 + 2 = 5\), \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(X = \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix} -4 & -5 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\tfrac{4}{5} & -1 \\ \tfrac{2}{5} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(AX = B \Rightarrow X = A^{-1}B\), where \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(|A| = 1(4-4) - 2(-4-2) + 3(-2-1) = 0 + 12 - 9 = 3 \neq 0\).

Cofactors give \(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & 1 & -5 \\ -3 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{3}\,\text{adj}(A)\).

\(X = \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & 1 & -5 \\ -3 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 0-4+3 \\ 6+2-15 \\ -3+0+9 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -7 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\tfrac{1}{3} \\ -\tfrac{7}{3} \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(AXB = C \Rightarrow X = A^{-1}CB^{-1}\), where \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 24 & 7 \\ 31 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(|A|=1\Rightarrow A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\); \(|B|=1\Rightarrow B^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1}C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 24 & 7 \\ 31 & 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 17 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(X = \begin{bmatrix} 17 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = 1(4-4) - 2(-4-2) + 3(-2-1) = 12 - 9 = 3 \neq 0\).

Adjoint method — cofactors give
\(\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & 1 & -5 \\ -3 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & 1 & -5 \\ -3 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

Elementary transformations — writing \(A = IA\) and row-reducing \(A\) to \(I\) (using \(R_2 \to R_2 + R_1,\ R_3 \to R_3 - R_1\), then clearing) yields the identical result
\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & 1 & -5 \\ -3 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

Both methods agree.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = 1(2-6) + 1(0-2) = -6 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

Write \(A = AI\) and reduce \(A\) (on the left) to \(I\) using column transformations; the same operations applied to \(I\) (on the right) build \(A^{-1}\). Carrying this out gives
\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 & 2 \\ -3 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)
(matching the adjoint result for the same matrix).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = -1 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

Write \(A = IA\) and reduce \(A\) to \(I\) by row transformations (\(R_2 \to R_2 - R_1,\ R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1\), then clear the remaining entries); the matrix that accumulates on the right of \(I\) is \(A^{-1}\):
\(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 2 & -7 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)
(matching the adjoint result of Q.14 for the same matrix).

Let \(A = [a_{ij}]_{3\times3}\) with cofactors \(A_{ij}\). The expression
\(a_{11}A_{21} + a_{12}A_{22} + a_{13}A_{23}\)
multiplies the entries of row 1 by the cofactors of row 2.

By the property of \("alien cofactors\)": the sum of products of the elements of one row with the cofactors of a DIFFERENT row is \(0\). Equivalently, this sum equals the determinant of the matrix obtained by replacing row 2 of \(A\) with a copy of row 1 — that matrix has two identical rows, so its determinant is \(0\).

Hence \(a_{11}A_{21} + a_{12}A_{22} + a_{13}A_{23} = 0\).

Let \(A = [a_{ij}]_{3\times3}\) with cofactors \(A_{ij}\). The expression
\(a_{11}A_{11} + a_{12}A_{12} + a_{13}A_{13}\)
multiplies the entries of row 1 by the cofactors of the SAME row 1.

This is precisely the expansion of the determinant of \(A\) along row 1.

Hence \(a_{11}A_{11} + a_{12}A_{12} + a_{13}A_{13} = |A|\).

\(XA = B \Rightarrow X = BA^{-1}\), where \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\).

From Q.15, \(|A| = -6\) and \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 & 2 \\ -3 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(X = B A^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 & 2 \\ -3 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 & 2 \\ 11 & 8 & -5 \\ 10 & 10 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
